4: Compare five materials and their reference temperatures, then examine O-rings, complete-fitting temperatures and pressure ratings. Use these distinctions to select fittings, seals and tubing and plan validation before service.
5: Start fitting material selection with the properties of the material itself.
6: Start fitting material selection with the properties of the material itself. PP has low density and resists many aqueous solutions; PA offers strength, toughness and wear resistance; POM combines stiffness, low friction and dimensional stability; PVDF offers chemical resistance; PEEK combines elevated-temperature performance, strength and chemical resistance. Evaluate the actual fluid, temperature, pressure and mechanical loading.
7: Compare explicit temperature and pressure values. Material reference upper limits are PP 110°C, PA 120°C, POM 100°C, PVDF 150°C and PEEK 225°C. In contrast, a Q20 fitting with PP body and EPDM seal has an upper operating temperature of 71°C and a listed working pressure of 120 psi (approximately 0.83 MPa). Material properties and complete-fitting requirements are discussed separately below.
8: Validate under actual operating conditions before service.
9: Validate under actual operating conditions before service. Sealing and life depend on fluid identity/concentration, temperature, pressure and fluctuations, contact time, cleaning, seals, tubing and assembly. These values support initial selection, not replacement of actual tests. Before installation or production use, test the chosen model within its permitted conditions with the intended fluid, seals and tubing.
10: How do PP, PA, POM, PVDF and PEEK fitting materials differ?
11: Compare chemical resistance, mechanical properties, moisture-related dimensional change and temperature capability. Chemical resistance means resisting chemical exposure while retaining properties. The temperature table supports initial material selection; resin type/formulation, fluid, loading and duration affect suitability. Its limits are not continuous operating ratings for complete fittings.
16: Low density; resists many aqueous solutions. Candidate for aqueous reagent and rinse lines after compatibility confirmation
18: Strength, toughness and wear resistance; candidate for mechanically loaded connections, considering dimensional change after water absorption
20: Stiffness, low friction and low water absorption; candidate for repeatedly connected or sliding components
22: Chemical resistance with mechanical strength; candidate for corrosive reagent and chemical-sample lines
24: Elevated-temperature capability and strength; candidate for higher-temperature or load-bearing requirements
25: Lower limits are also material reference values, not proof of reliable fitting sealing at that temperature. For cold service, test body, seals and tubing together.
26: PP: low density and suitability for many aqueous fluid paths
27: PP resists many salt solutions, alkalis and weak acids. PP barbed or thread-to-barb fittings can be candidates for aqueous reagents, rinsing and reservoir-to-tubing connections, subject to compatibility with the actual fluid.
28: Focus on fluid identity and sustained loading. Oxidizing cleaners, some organic solvents and elevated temperatures require separate assessment. Tube tension or thread compression can cause deformation affecting fit and sealing. Successful ambient-water service does not establish suitability after hot cleaning.
29: PA: strength, toughness and wear resistance
30: PA can be considered for assembly loads, tubing tension or repeated friction because of its mechanical properties. Still provide proper tubing support to reduce external loads on the fitting.
31: PA absorbs moisture from air and may absorb water from aqueous media, changing dimensions and mechanical properties. This can affect thread engagement and barb retention. PA6, PA66 and PA12 are distinct polyamides; 'nylon' does not make them interchangeable.
32: Even one polyamide type has different resin grades. A grade identifies a material supplier's formulation/product, not the fitting model. Confirm grade, reinforcement or modification, then test dimensional and property changes after moisture absorption and actual-fluid exposure.
33: POM: stiffness, low friction and dimensional stability
34: POM's stiffness, wear resistance, low friction and low water absorption help maintain dimensions and clearances. Consider it for quick disconnect or sliding components, while checking actual wetted fluids and loads.
35: Mechanical properties do not replace compatibility testing. Assess strong acids, strong oxidizers and chlorine-containing cleaners particularly carefully. Smooth dry operation does not prove retained fit or sealing after immersion or repeated cleaning.
36: PVDF: chemical resistance with mechanical strength
37: PVDF is a fluoropolymer resistant to many acids, salts and other chemicals. It is a candidate for corrosive reagents or chemical samples; also confirm that the required configuration and size are available.
38: PVDF has limitations, notably with strong alkalis and particular organic solvents. Assess concentration, temperature and resin formulation. 'Fluoropolymer' does not mean compatible with every corrosive medium.
40: PEEK combines temperature capability, mechanical strength and chemical resistance. Consider PEEK fittings and mating parts for rigid tubing in analytical instruments or locations requiring higher temperature capability, strength and dimensional stability.
41: PEEK is not universal: concentrated sulfuric acid and strong oxidizers need particular scrutiny. Resin temperature capability does not establish a finished fitting's operating temperature or pressure rating. Threads, wall thickness, port structure and tubing must all suit the duty.
42: A 121°C cleaning requirement exceeds the table's PP 110°C, PA 120°C and POM 100°C reference limits. PVDF 150°C and PEEK 225°C exceed 121°C, but still require confirmation of finished-fitting temperature limits, cleaning fluid and duration. Passing initial material screening is not validation for 121°C cleaning or sterilization.
43: Why must O-ring material be selected separately from the fitting body?
44: After the body, examine the sealing structure. Some fittings use O-rings, gaskets or other seals. An O-ring quick disconnect closes the mating gap through seal compression; a one-piece barb mainly relies on the tube wall conforming to its surface. Not every fitting requires an added O-ring.
45: Body and seal have different functions and may use different materials. For a PP body with EPDM (ethylene propylene diene rubber), confirm both against the same fluid and cleaning conditions. Seal swelling, hardening or insufficient elastic recovery after compression can cause leakage or difficult connection even if the body looks intact.
46: Operating temperature depends on the combined body, seals and other parts. The table gives Q20/Q40 values for PP+EPDM and POM+NBR (nitrile rubber). These are finished-fitting values, not universal temperature ranges for EPDM or NBR.
50: Q20 / Q40 | PP body + EPDM seal
51: Finished fitting upper limit 71°C, not the PP reference limit of 110°C
52: Q20 / Q40 | POM body + NBR seal
53: Finished fitting upper limit 82°C, not the POM reference limit of 100°C
54: Cleaning at 80°C exceeds the 71°C limit for Q20/Q40 PP+EPDM. POM+NBR has an 82°C upper limit, but cleaning chemistry, temperature variation and pressure still need confirmation. Changing to FKM fluoroelastomer seals requires reassessment of the complete fitting's permitted temperature and pressure; do not copy the old combination or a rubber-material table.
55: Confirm seal formulation, dimensions, hardness and assembly. In valved fittings, trace the fluid path to identify internal wetted parts. For rigid-tube fittings, distinguish sleeves, ferrules and washers by material and function. A component is wetted if it contacts the fluid; whether an external retainer is wetted depends on the actual construction.

76: How do you assess compatibility with reagents and cleaning fluids?
77: List every fluid: process liquid, cleaner, disinfectant, rinse and mixtures remaining during shutdown. 'Acid', 'alkali' or 'alcohol' is insufficient. Concentration, temperature and contact time can change the conclusion for the same chemical.
78: Record chemical identity and concentration; for mixtures, state major components and proportions using the actual formulation or product data.
79: List operating and cleaning temperature, contact time, frequency and any prolonged shutdown immersion separately.
80: Use compatibility information for initial screening, then confirm the resin, actual components and complete assembly. Missing compatibility data is not approval.
81: Validate actual samples for mixtures, changing temperatures or sustained loads, including seals and tubing.
82: A line carrying ambient aqueous liquid and periodically cleaned with a chlorine-containing agent cannot be assessed for water alone. Record the cleaner's active ingredients, concentration, temperature and contact time, then check body, seal and tubing. Repeated cleaning may change these parts and cause a previously sound joint to leak.

86: What pressure can fittings withstand, and how do quick disconnects compare with dedicated high-pressure fittings?
87: Pressure capability depends on structure, materials and mating parts. Q20/Q40 PP and POM fittings list 120 psi (approximately 0.83 MPa); Q60 PP lists 60 psi (approximately 0.41 MPa). Even the same PP material has different ratings across series.
92: Temperature range −20 to 71°C; confirm allowable pressure at the target temperature
93: Temperature range −40 to 82°C; confirm allowable pressure at the target temperature
95: For the listed Q60 fittings; do not apply Q20/Q40's 120 psi
96: Dedicated high-pressure fitting family | 10-32 UNF coned port
98: Limit of that dedicated family, not every PEEK or rigid-tube fitting
99: MPa values are rounded conversions from psi. Evaluate pressure and temperature together; do not assume maximum pressure is permitted at maximum temperature. Confirm each model's pressure at the target temperature, then test with actual fluid, seals and tubing, including start/stop transients, cleaning and sustained operation. For cold Q60 service, confirm the lower temperature limit of the exact mating models.
100: At a required 0.60 MPa, Q60's 60 psi (approximately 0.41 MPa) is insufficient despite its larger bore. Q20/Q40's 120 psi (approximately 0.83 MPa) exceeds 0.60 MPa, but suitability still depends on flow, temperature, fluid and peak pressure. For dedicated high-pressure fittings, match model, tubing and port; 34 MPa is not a generic PEEK rating.
101: Installation torque also depends on the high-pressure fitting material
102: For that dedicated high-pressure structure, listed assembly torques are 0.45 N·m for PEEK and 2.2 N·m for metal. Confirm the exact model; do not apply these values to ordinary barbs or other ferrule fittings. Additional tightening cannot increase the pressure rating.
103: Under sustained loading, plastic deformation can increase with time: creep. Temperature and fluid affect it. For face-contact seals, check retained compression after service; for barbs, inspect tubing softening, loosening and movement. A satisfactory ambient assembly check does not replace post-operation testing.
107: Allowable pressure of fitting and tubing at the target temperature
109: Leakage or loosening after repeated temperature/pressure changes and alternating fluids
111: Torque, tool and sealing method for the material and structure
113: Tubing dimensions, hardness, expansion during insertion and restraint

128: How should fittings be tested under actual conditions before service?
129: Test the intended purchased model with its actual seals, tubing and mating parts using real fluid, temperature, pressure and cleaning. Identical material names can conceal different formulations, dimensions or assembly. Test the complete fitting and tubing combination.
130: Preparation: record complete model, drawing revision, body/seal materials, tubing and assembly; define test conditions and acceptance criteria for the duty.
131: Fluid exposure: use actual formulation, concentration, temperature and time; inspect appearance, dimensions and properties. For analytical circuits, assess extractables or fluid residues that could interfere with measurement as required by the project.
132: Connection tests: assemble actual flexible or rigid tubing and mating parts as specified; check leakage, pull-off resistance and flow at intended temperature/pressure, adding repeated disconnection if required.
133: After operation: simulate starts/stops, continuous duty and cleaning within model limits; recheck sealing, loosening and deformation. Record batch, duration and results.
134: Define duration, cycles and acceptance criteria beforehand. A brief leak test does not establish long-term service life. Changes to body material, seals, tubing, assembly or cleaning require reassessment and relevant tests before use.
136: What is the pressure rating of PA, PVDF or ordinary PEEK fittings?
137: Material name alone cannot establish it. Q20/Q40 120 psi, Q60 60 psi and the dedicated high-pressure family's 34 MPa apply to their specific products or family. Confirm the chosen model and tubing ratings and validate actual conditions before service.
138: Can a fitting specified only as PA be purchased as PA66?
139: No. PA is the polyamide family, not a specific PA6, PA66 or other type. Confirm resin grade, reinforcement and modifications with the supplier and state them in purchasing requirements. Moisture absorption and mechanical properties may differ.
140: Can a plastic fitting simply be replaced with stainless steel?
141: Recheck the complete connection: steel grade, surface, fluid compatibility, threads, sealing faces, tubing fit and installation. Matching names or appearance do not establish interchangeability, and plastic-fitting torque must not be reused automatically.
142: Select fitting materials for the actual fluid and duty
143: Provide fluid and concentration, operating/cleaning temperatures, pressure, contact time, tubing and connection structure to identify candidates and pre-service testing.
